title: I was seventeen when I found out my father had been secretly planning my future without telling me, and the worst part wasn’t the betrayal

blocks.text: In the 1550s, a young woman in the Italian city of Cremona picked up a brush and painted a laughing girl so vividly that the drawing found its way into the hands of Michelangelo. He looked at it and said he would like to see her portray a weeping boy. She did, and he was reportedly impressed. Her name was Sofonisba Anguissola, and she would go on to become one of the first internationally celebrated female painters in history—a court painter to King Philip II of Spain, admired by Van Dyck, and yet today almost forgotten.

Born around 1531, Sofonisba was the eldest of seven children in the Anguissola family of Piacenza. Her father, Amilcare, was a respected nobleman and a busy figure in Cremona’s civic life. The family liked to claim it descended from a warrior named Suardi Galvano, who had helped liberate Constantinople in the eighth century and reportedly cried out, “Anguis sola fecit victoriam”—the snake alone brought victory. The emperor rewarded him with the family name Anguissola.

Sofonisba would weave that serpent emblem into her self-portraits for the rest of her career, never letting anyone forget her noble status. The household was unusual. Amilcare and his wife Bianca had six daughters and only one son, and rather than raising the girls in the ordinary way, they gave them a humanist education normally reserved for boys. Sofonisba and her sister Elena began studying painting when she was about eleven, first under Bernardino Campi. When he moved to Milan a few years later, their father simply found them another teacher. This was extraordinary. Women were generally only allowed to study art within the family circle, but Sofonisba became the first known female painter to apprentice outside her own home. Amilcare managed his daughters’ talents like a careful businessman. Painting was supposed to be a noble pastime for girls, not a profession, but he understood the opportunity. He corresponded with leading artists and thinkers, sending examples of Sofonisba’s work to powerful people, always presenting her as a virtuous noblewoman who happened to possess remarkable skill. The strategy worked. Giorgio Vasari, the famous art historian, visited the family home in Cremona in 1566 and wrote admiringly of the four Anguissola sisters as a shining example of artistic cultivation.

One of Sofonisba’s earliest surviving masterpieces is a scene of three of her sisters playing chess, with a servant watching over them. It has been called the first everyday domestic scene in Italian painting. In it, the elegantly dressed eldest sister, Lucia, turns to the viewer while young Europa smiles and Minerva gestures eagerly. The painting radiated refinement and learning, and it hung prominently in the family house for visitors to admire. Another portrait showed their father Amilcare with his hand placed lovingly on the shoulder of their brother Asdrubale, the long-awaited male heir marking the family’s continuity. Sofonisba had no formal anatomical training—women were barred from such study—and her figures sometimes showed awkward proportions, but her gift for conveying intelligence, spirit, and family bonds was undeniable. When Sofonisba was still a teenager, her reputation began to spread. At fifteen, she was praised by a local bishop as one of the most talented painters who had ever lived. By the time she was in her twenties, she was mentioned in printed verse alongside other cultured noblewomen. A contemporary intellectual begged her father for a portrait of her, saying he wanted to show two wonders at once: the painting and the painter herself. There was one problem. A woman of her rank was expected to marry, but Amilcare admitted he had no dowry to give her.

The matter simply remained unresolved. Then the opportunity of a lifetime arrived. Around her twenty-fifth year, in 1559, Sofonisba was invited to the Spanish court to serve as a lady-in-waiting to the young future queen, Elisabeth of Valois, the fourteen-year-old French princess who was to marry King Philip II. The Duke of Alba had recommended her. Philip agreed to pay her salary and provide her dowry. Amilcare, though heartbroken to send his beloved daughter so far away, wrote to the King expressing his devotion and entrusted her to the greatest monarch in the Christian world. That autumn Sofonisba set out for Spain with a small entourage, carrying chests of her finest clothes and letters of passage that let her move through the various ports and checkpoints along the route. She sailed to Barcelona, crossed Catalonia and Castile, and finally reached Guadalajara, where the young queen was expected.

During the wedding celebrations, she made a memorable appearance at the evening ball. When no one dared to begin the dance ordered by the King, some said she led the way. Other reports placed her at the climax of the festivities, the torch dance, when she was chosen to hand the ceremonial torch to Philip II himself—a symbolic act marking the dawn of a promising new reign. From the spring of 1561, the court settled in Madrid, at the Alcázar, which Philip had chosen as his new capital.

Sofonisba took her place in the Casa de la Reina, the official household of the Queen. This was a paid position and a serious honor. The ladies-in-waiting lived by strict rules, sharing the private quarters of the royal women while keeping their distance from the outside world. Their day began with the elaborate ceremony of dressing the Queen, choosing jewelry, gowns, and hairstyles meant to impress the King and the court. Then the Queen, surrounded by her ladies and accompanied by Princess Juana, the King’s sister, would attend Mass. Sofonisba received a regular salary, though payment was not always prompt. At one point she had to demand back pay. Sofonisba did more than serve the Queen. She also became Elisabeth’s painting teacher. The Queen showed such quick progress under her Italian lady’s instruction that even her mother, Catherine de’ Medici, heard about it with astonishment. Sofonisba’s first portrait of Elisabeth was so admired that Philip himself commissioned a copy. The Queen insisted it was painted from life and produced with such near-supernatural perfection that both she and the King were delighted.

Sofonisba painted at least three portraits of Elisabeth, and perhaps many more copies and variations. Nearly all of them were lost in devastating palace fires, one in 1604 at El Pardo and another in 1734 at the Alcázar, which together destroyed around five hundred paintings. Sixty-five works by Sofonisba may have perished in those flames. The portraits that survive today in museum collections, including one in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna signed with her married name, likely derive from her lost originals. She even painted Don Carlos, the King’s tragic and disfigured son. He wanted to be shown standing, dressed in a deerskin coat lined with wolf fur, and Sofonisba did everything she could to soften his physical deformities. His back was badly curved, his legs uneven, and his face far from handsome, but her portrait satisfied him so completely that he later ordered six copies in her style. That original portrait has since vanished. Only nine years after her arrival in Spain, Sofonisba’s world turned upside down. In 1568, Don Carlos died, and a few months later, Queen Elisabeth died during a difficult pregnancy, along with her unborn child. The entire court dissolved into grief. Sofonisba, deeply attached to her young mistress, fell into a depression so severe that one letter recorded she said she no longer wanted to live.

Once the Queen’s household was disbanded, its members were reassigned, sent home, pushed into marriages or convents. Some stayed to serve the infant princesses, and Sofonisba remained near the royal daughters, though her exact position grew unclear. She waited, anxious, as the King decided what to do with her. He apparently felt she had stayed at court long enough and began arranging for her departure. Sofonisba resented being sent away. Around this time, she joined other ladies in a strange act of rebellion. The King had ordered padlocks installed on the windows of the ladies’ quarters, presumably so that the young women could not look out or signal to gallants below. One night, Sofonisba and several other ladies tore out the door bolts and smashed the window locks, then threatened to beat the heads of anyone who tried to lock them in again. Philip was furious and ordered them sent home without their dowries. He confined them to their rooms, but Queen Anna, his new wife, who had befriended Sofonisba, interceded and had them freed after only half a day. The King felt the punishment had been far too short. In the end, Philip had his way about Sofonisba’s future.

In 1572 a husband was finally found for her: Fabrizio Moncada, the second son of a Sicilian prince, roughly her own age. The proxy wedding took place in the chapel of the Alcázar in June 1573, in the presence of the Queen, the princesses, and the whole royal family. Sofonisba wore a dress embroidered with pearls worth nine hundred scudi, and afterward she sailed to Sicily with her new husband. In Sicily she continued to paint, but her work became more intimate and devotional, turning away from the splendor of court portraiture. She had brought a large dowry of over twenty thousand ducats, but Fabrizio was perpetually in debt. He constantly took out loans and pawned her possessions to maintain his lavish lifestyle, including a silver-embroidered cloth and an enameled gold ring set with a large square diamond, very likely the ring Don Carlos had given her in gratitude for the portrait that had hidden his deformities. She never recovered it. The marriage lasted only five years. On April 25, 1578, Fabrizio boarded a ship bound for Spain, perhaps seeking the King’s financial help. Pirates attacked near the island of Capri. In the panic and disorder, as the crew and passengers abandoned ship, the single man to drown was Don Fabrizio Moncada. Sofonisba found herself widowed and financially vulnerable.

She now needed a male guardian to recover her dowry, since a woman in that era had almost no legal standing of her own. Philip II offered to let her return to Spain, but she chose instead to return to Italy and seek help from her brother Asdrubale, who supported her and acted as her legal representative. Then came what some might call her boldest move. In 1579, just a year after her husband’s death, Sofonisba and her brother set sail from Palermo to Genoa aboard a ship commanded by a man named Orazio Lomellini, fifteen years younger than she and of lower rank, though from a respected Genoese family. The two fell in love. Word reached Grand Duke Francesco de’ Medici in Tuscany, who wrote to her in friendship, discouraging her from doing something that would displease her relatives and dishonor her family’s standing. He also pointed out that she had no permission from the King. She married Orazio anyway. The move to Genoa marked a new chapter. Surrounded by artists and writers, Sofonisba picked up her brush again, making new friends while never forgetting the Spanish court that had treated her generously. She encountered old royal connections there as well. When Maria of Austria, daughter of Charles V and sister of Philip II, passed through Genoa in 1581, Sofonisba gave her a painting of the Virgin Mary, which Maria prized.

In 1583 she finally received compensation for the hardships caused by Moncada’s death—a yearly pension that gave the couple a dignified living. In 1585 she met the Infanta Catalina Michaela again, Elisabeth of Valois’s second daughter, accompanying her toward her wedding in Turin and making sketches for a portrait of the bride. In 1599 she met Catalina’s older sister, Isabella Clara Eugenia, who was traveling to the Netherlands to rule there with her husband. After thirty-five years in Genoa, the couple returned to Palermo in 1615 because of Orazio’s business obligations. Sofonisba, now in her eighties, accompanied him. By then she had stopped painting because her eyesight was failing. Yet in July 1624, the young Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck came to visit her. In his Italian sketchbook he drew the ninety-six-year-old Sofonisba from life and wrote an admiring note about her. He praised her sharp memory, her lively mind, and her unfailing courtesy. In one passage he recorded her saying that her greatest sorrow was no longer being able to paint, though her hand remained perfectly steady. When he painted her portrait, she gave him practical advice, warning him not to make the light too strong because harsh shadows would bring out the wrinkles of age. Van Dyck’s sketchbook contains many studies from Italian travels, but his pages on Sofonisba are the longest and most personal entry in the more than two-hundred-page diary.

She is the only female artist he recorded there. Sofonisba died on November 16, 1625, in Palermo, without children. Orazio honored her with a marble tomb slab, calling her one of the most famous women in the world, unmatched in her era in portraying the human likeness, and wrote that no one of her time could equal her. He had two sons from earlier relationships, and Sofonisba had evidently been close to them. In 1620 she left her possessions to one of them, and later divided her inheritance between the two young men. Her story shows what talent and determination could achieve even in an age of extraordinary limits. Sofonisba Anguissola’s paintings found their way into major collections, from the Vatican to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, where her portrait of the Spanish royal family still hangs. She is seldom singled out, though she was celebrated in her lifetime as one of the most accomplished painters in Europe. She never gave up. When the world gave her almost no room, she made her own.
